verdict.reasoning: Duration and description supported: Doctor summarizes, “For the last four days, you've had very itchy skin, very sore skin all over your body, mainly your chest.” Patient earlier notes it is “sore, and a red skin… it's kind of, it's really itchy.”

Locations and absence on face supported: Patient says rash is on “mostly like my chest, my, my hands, my arms” and later clarifies “just the chest, hands and like, like inside the elbows.” When asked, “anything on your face at all?” patient answers “On my face? No.”

Impact on sleep, work, hiking supported: Patient says, “I can't even sleep at night… at work I can't focus… I'm always… disturbed by this disease,” and also, “I like, for instance hiking… I can't really do it anymore… because super painful… very very annoying.”

Dry, cracked skin without bleeding or discharge supported: Doctor notes, “you mentioned it's, you've got some dry skin and some, uh cracked skin as well,” and asks about “any other uh pus or blood…?” Patient replies “No,” and confirms no “pus or blood, coming out of your skin.”
Doctor asks, “have you noticed any temperature or fevers?” Patient replies, “No. just very itchy. Nothing else.”
Doctor asks, “So your, your bowels are working OK?” and there is no indication of problems; this is accepted as normal in context of ROS questioning.
Doctor asks, “Your chest is OK? No cough, no breathing difficulties?” Patient answers, “No.”
Doctor asks, “You're passing urine OK.” Patient replies, “I I think so.” This indicates no reported urinary issue.
Patient states, “earlier I was like prescribed for my eczema,” and later, “I had eczema before.”
When asked about other medical problems, patient says, “I just had asthma in the past. But not anymore.”
Doctor asks, “And do you take any regular medications at the moment?” Patient responds, “Uh no.”
Patient says, “I bought a, a steroid cream at the pharmacy last night. But it apparently didn't help, because it's still itching a lot today.”
Patient states, “Yes, I have tried antihistamines, uh lately, but it didn't really help.” and repeats, “I have tried uh antihistamines, but uh but it didn't really help.”
Doctor asks multiple times, “do you have any allergies at all?” Patient answers, “Ohh, allergies. Uh, no.”
Patient says, “I'm thirty one… I live with a few flatmates… I work uh at a pharmaceutical company… I'm a, like a kind of project manager.”
When asked, “do you smoke at all?” patient replies, “No.” For alcohol, patient says, “a few, a few beers per week… Nothing, nothing crazy.”

Doctor states, “based on everything you mentioned… I do wonder whether this is a flare-up of your eczema,” and notes the itchiness and distribution. This matches characterization of a likely eczema flare of a pruritic erythematous rash (erythema implied by patient description of “red skin”).
Patient links itch to sleep disturbance: “I can't even sleep at night… it's itching a lot, like all the time.” This supports that sleep disturbance is secondary to pruritus.
Doctor says, “I wonder whether giving you a stronger prescription of a of a steroid may be beneficial, which I'm happy to prescribe to you today.” Context is treatment of presumed eczema flare.
Doctor: “I'm going to give you something, some emollients… which use in the bath and shower… definitely worth um using that for the first seven to ten days.”

Doctor advises, “It's also worth um using antihistamines… Things like Loratadine or Piriton,” and later, “I can give you something a little bit stronger today as well. Um, something like Fexofenadine, which I can give to you today. It's definitely worth trying.”
Doctor instructs, “it's also worth keeping a diary of any triggers which are affecting your symptoms, anything you wear or anything you use, in terms of shower gels or soap.”
Transcript only states, “do come back and see me next week, if things don't get better.” There is no mention of returning earlier for worsening or new symptoms, so that part is added.
